questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to experience how the legal world is in the US and be amongst American legal professors and students - I want to work internationally so I was also curious of the possibility of studying and working abroad

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had an amazing time and would 10/10 do it again.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: There is a lot of things to do in preparation for going on exchange but it was overall easy to find information. The university had an orientation day just for us exchange students to know our way around the university and understand everything that was important. They took really good care of us.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The Global Programs team in the school welcomed us and gave us all the relevant information and gave us a tour of the university and told us about each function of the different offices in the school so we always knew who to go to for further questions. We also got a mentor that we could write to and hang out with.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Very satisfied. However, in the acceptance letter there were two orientation days - a Thursday and a Friday. But there were no activities on the Friday, so we had to organize ourselves which was fine, but it would have been nice that the university organized something for us - also with other students across the international program.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
It's easy if you have money. San Francisco is very expensive so there are a lot of options if you have money. 
Sharing rooms is normal to save money. I lived with my classmade in a pretty sizeable room in a big house for $850 a month. 
We were lucky that we didn't have to pay deposit or utilities, but usually you have to. 
Airbnb is also an option for the first couple of months.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Living off campus is the best option. The university is in the homeless area - the area is pretty safe in the day, but in the night it can get a bit dodgy. So areas like the Richmond, The Haight/Ashbury, the Marina, Folsom Street, Sunset, The Castro and Russian Hill is very nice and safe. But stay away from Tenderloin, Civic Center, Market Street and Mission District.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: You can live on campus in Academe but it's $2000 for a small room. It's brand new and good quality, but you can definitely find something less expensive in a better area. The host university does not help you were much neither finding accommodation.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It's good, but also stressful because you can drop and add courses the first week, so you get a change to test the courses before you commit. Some courses also have a waitlist and some become available and others don't. Everything worked out for me, but the course I was most excited about was really boring, so I had to move my courses around last minute.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: They open the courses around 1 month before on the university platform and then you have to register. The courses register right away so you can see what book to buy and read for each course in Canvas. The registration process is good and works well. You can also see how many people are allowed in each courses and if there is a waitlist, you can keep an eye on where you are on the waitlist.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Registar's Office was available or the Global Programs team.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was successful in getting what I wanted, but the biggest issue was the schedule of the courses. Most of the courses I wanted, was scheduled at the same time, so I had to make some sacrifices. I also didn't want to have classes after dark, because I didn't want to take the bus home in the night.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Make sure that the courses you want are actually being offered and check you are looking at the right semester (fall or spring) and then select them and have a look at the schedule. When the registration opens, then you have them ready to just press "register now".

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I loved it all and learned so much.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Some classes are harder than others and also depends on the professor and what they expect of you. The teachers who expect more are generally also the courses that you learn more from and work harder for. Any class with Professor Keith Hand is challenging but it's so worth it. I also had a practical course of negotiations which was less legal theory and more how to act strategic and use negotiation methods to become a good negotiator.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
US is famous for socratic method (cold calling) so always be prepared because it's normal that the teacher ask you without you raising your hand. You learn to think on your feet and the more prepared you are, the more you can follow the class discussions. They also take attendance.
DO NOT go on exchange in the US and expect a vacation - you will need to attend and prepare for most courses. Within the first two weeks you will know in what classes you don't have to prepare as much and which courses you need to be on your feet.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: I had immigration law, environmental law, international business transactions and negotiations.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: International business transactions and negotiations - see above.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: There is an administration fee of $700 that we suddenly had to pay in the first couple of weeks and you don't really know what it's for and why. But the university arranged a lot of trips for us (baseball games, barbeques, Alcatraz trip, Halloween party) so I have an idea that maybe the money was spend for this, because we didn't pay for these trips.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Supermarket and housing is expensive. All things you buy in US does not have tax and tips included, so you have to get used to the price not being the final price. Some places in San Francisco are more relaxed about tipping and others are not. It's ok not to tip if you are getting a to-go coffee in my opinion.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The Global Programs arranged a lot of nice things for us to do as a group. The university also have a weekly news letter online where they arrange a lot of law related events.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Legal lectures, Presidential Watch Party, hanging out in bars, emotional support dog, welcome party on the beach

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Depend on what you are interested in they have many guest lectures which are interesting

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Explore California - go to Yosemite, Oakland, Sausalito, Stanford University, Berkeley, Joshua Tree, drive to LA 
Explore San Francisco and all it's nice areas. I dance salsa in my freetime so I explore all the salsa parties around the city. Don't be afraid to go out alone and talk to locals. If you want to experience the LGBTQ+ area, go to Castro; it's a nice area in the day and also in the night. 
Valencia St is my favourite street!! Baker Beach is beautiful and walking to Lands End and seeing the Golden gate is amazing.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: So easy. The students and Americans in general are so nice and open, so it was easy to fit in and bond.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Make at least one friend in each course you have and then go for coffee with them or hang out in your space time. Don't be afraid to put yourself out there. I didn't focus so much on the other international students; I was more focused in bonding with the Americans as this is the point of exchange

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: All the American students are used to the cold-calling culture in the class so they always know how to keep calm and speak their mind. that's very different from the university culture here.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The openness and confidence when they speak

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Be prepared that you will spend a lot of money - I went without SU and I still managed to have a good time, but go with enough money, so you don't have to compromise yourself. 
2) Be prepared that you have to pay 15,000 DKK in insurance to the university and it's hard to waive it. I have Tryg insurance and I got it waived after a lot of frustration and stress, but don't give up. 
3) Choose courses that allow you the possibility to get an LLM (Master of law) and choose courses that are mandatory for the bar exam in the US in case you want to come back or work as an attorney in US

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: You can borrow the books you need in the library for free for 3 hours at a time. I did not buy books at all, so it saved me a lot of money.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
That I went alone and loved it as much as I did. I made a home for myself and got to know a lot of people around the city. There was always somewhere to go and Americans are very sweet and open so there is always an opportunity for you to try something new and make friends. 
The university life was a big part of my experience as well. I loved going to class and never felt exhausted from school.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Getting into the legal language in English and following class, but once I found my technique, it was easy. If you are used to communicating in English, you will find it easy to adapt but it can be a bit challenging if you are not that used to speaking English.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer:
I went on exchange without SU so I had to find ways to save money in a lot of areas, but I was lucky to find someone to share a room with. Scholarships are not the easiest to get and I only got one scholarship of 10.000 DKK out of applying for more than 20. 
For anyone who wants to go, you need around 150.000-200.000 for the whole semester if you want to have financial freedom. You can do with less, but it's a once-in-a-lifetime experience, so you shouldn't compromise if you want to take weekend trips and buying that extra beer :)

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
